entries.name: Accelerant Twister, LLC et al. v. Marjo, LLC and John T. Sullivan

arguments_rejected_or_waived: License Agreement void for lack of consideration or "actual fraud" (Twister and Holding, invoking 8 Del. C. § 152 case law): rejected. Assuming arguendo the corporate doctrine applies to an LLC (fn. 187 expressly does not so hold), Twister received an exclusive license it used to build machines and raise capital, and consideration is measured at formation, not by later commercial disappointment.

Missing written assignment under 35 U.S.C. § 261 as failure of consideration, material breach, or misrepresentation rendering the agreement voidable: rejected. The breach of § 3.1 was technical and immaterial, Twister got the benefit of its bargain, no adverse claim arose, and Borom knew Sullivan was the named inventor, so there was no inducement or reasonable reliance.

Failure to give advance copies of patent filings under § 4.1 as a material breach justifying termination under § 6.11(b): rejected. Twister had no veto, no damages were shown, Twister kept accepting the agreement's benefits for years, and the termination grounds were pretextual.

Section 6.11(d) acceleration and equipment return apply only when Marjo terminates for non-payment: rejected as contrary to the unambiguous "or for any other reason" language; December 2019 negotiation drafts and emails are inadmissible extrinsic evidence.

Fiduciary claim impermissibly bootstrapped to the § 8.10(i) contract claim: rejected. The contract claim turns on whether 25% interest is "compensation of any kind"; the fiduciary claim turns on conflicted self-dealing, an independent basis.

Broz does not apply to capital raising, and Twister could not raise capital because of the Dilution Protected Units: rejected. Broz translates to financing opportunities, and the record (the initial $1.24 million raise, no attempted second raise, Ellman's non-credible testimony, Holding's raises on Twister's assets) contradicted the claimed inability.

Anderson's $10.756 million damages model: rejected because it valued Twister at $0 and allocated 100% of projected cash flows to Holding while Marjo kept its 16.3% Twister stake; the Court adopted Greco's corrected $462,000 figure.

Holding does not breach § 4.9 because it collects PaaS revenue for Twister at no mark-up under "subscriptions": rejected. The covenant asks whether an affiliate operates in the cone-rolling equipment market, not whether it competes with Twister, and Holding is Twister's parent, not a wholly owned subsidiary.

Marjo's contention that the July 2021 unit exchange required 90% member approval under § 8.10(i): rejected. Article X (§§ 10.01(a), 10.04(a)) specifically governs transfers and restructurings and controls over the general § 8.10(i); a Board majority sufficed.

Both sides' fee requests: rejected. Neither side was the overall "prevailing party" under § 15.14 given the split decision, and Twister and Holding's renewed bad-faith request (eve-of-trial claim withdrawal, witness-availability and phone-collection issues) lacked clear evidence of bad faith; unclean hands declined in the Court's discretion (fn. 562).

authorities_cited.proposition: Termination for cause requires an uncured material breach; termination "for any other reason" accelerates payment obligations with 18% interest after notice and a 15-day cure, and triggers return of equipment built using Patent-Related Technology; § 4.9 bars affiliates from the cone-rolling equipment market for three years after termination.

90% member vote for affiliate compensation arrangements; Board-majority authority over unit transfers and restructurings; member confidentiality; fiduciary duties eliminated except for Board members acting in that capacity; prevailing-party fees.

State courts lack jurisdiction over claims arising under patent law; a patent issue that is necessarily raised, actually disputed, substantial and federally resolvable divests the Court of jurisdiction over the PRO2/PRO4 return request and the parallel declaratory claim.

authorities_cited.authority: 17 U.S.C. § 301(a); OpenRisk, LLC v. MicroStrategy Servs. Corp., 876 F.3d 518 (4th Cir. 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: A conversion claim resting on copying of a copyrightable work (source code) and assertion of authorship is equivalent to copyright infringement and preempted.

authorities_cited.authority: Broz v. Cellular Info. Sys., Inc., 673 A.2d 148 (Del. 1996)
authorities_cited.proposition: Four-factor corporate opportunity test; a fiduciary does not usurp an opportunity the company is financially unable to exploit (applied to reject the CFG-line usurpation theory in fn. 456).

authorities_cited.authority: Metro Storage Int'l LLC v. Harron, 275 A.3d 810 (Del. Ch. 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: The corporate opportunity doctrine applies to opportunities to obtain financing, with the Broz factors adapted; supports imputation of a fiduciary's knowledge to controlled entities.

authorities_cited.authority: Deane v. Maginn, 2022 WL 16557974 (Del. Ch. Nov. 1, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: Direct pro rata recovery to minority LLC members on a derivative loyalty claim where entity-level recovery would return funds to the wrongdoers; self-serving claims of financial inability rejected; damages uncertainty resolved against the wrongdoer.

authorities_cited.authority: Weinberger v. UOP, Inc., 457 A.2d 701 (Del. 1983)
authorities_cited.proposition: A fiduciary on both sides bears the burden of entire fairness (fair dealing and fair price); directors of parent and subsidiary owe duties to both; broad remedial discretion.

authorities_cited.authority: William Penn P'ship v. Saliba, 13 A.3d 749 (Del. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: LLC managers owe traditional fiduciary duties absent express modification, and entire fairness applies where managers stand on both sides.

authorities_cited.authority: DeMarie v. Neff, 2005 WL 89403 (Del. Ch. Jan. 12, 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: A nonmaterial breach does not excuse performance; a party may not accept a contract's benefits while asserting it is void.

authorities_cited.authority: N. Am. Fire Ultimate Hldgs., LP v. Doorly, 2026 WL 274647 (Del. Feb. 3, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Consideration is measured at formation and not reevaluated at enforcement; unmet expectations do not show a lack of consideration.

authorities_cited.authority: DCV Hldgs., Inc. v. ConAgra, Inc., 889 A.2d 954 (Del. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: A specific provision (Article X) controls over a general one (§ 8.10(i)).

authorities_cited.authority: Aqua Flame, Inc. v. Imperial Fountains, Inc., 463 F. Supp. 736 (N.D. Tex. 1979)
authorities_cited.proposition: The licensor had no interest to convey because the inventor had assigned the patent to a bank; here Twister received its bargained-for rights.

authorities_cited.authority: Kent Jewelry Corp. v. Kiefer, 119 N.Y.S.2d 242 (Sup. Ct. N.Y. Cnty. 1952)
authorities_cited.proposition: The assignment to the licensor was void, so the licensee acquired no rights; not the case here.

authorities_cited.authority: In re El Paso Pipeline P'rs, L.P. Deriv. Litig., 132 A.3d 67 (Del. Ch. 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Pro rata recovery on a derivative claim in exceptional circumstances.

authorities_cited.authority: Osborn ex rel. Osborn v. Kemp, 991 A.2d 1153 (Del. 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Contract formation elements; read the contract as a whole without surplusage.

authorities_cited.authority: Eagle Indus., Inc. v. DeVilbiss Health Care, Inc., 702 A.2d 1228 (Del. 1997)
authorities_cited.proposition: No extrinsic evidence to interpret an unambiguous contract.

authorities_cited.authority: BioLife Sols., Inc. v. Endocare, Inc., 838 A.2d 268 (Del. Ch. 2003)
authorities_cited.proposition: Untimely delivery of patent files was not a material breach.

authorities_cited.authority: Nemec v. Shrader, 991 A.2d 1120 (Del. 2010); PT China LLC v. PT Korea LLC, 2010 WL 761145 (Del. Ch. Feb. 26, 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Contract-governed disputes are treated as contract claims unless the fiduciary claim has an independent basis.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Mindbody, Inc. S'holder Litig., 332 A.3d 349 (Del. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Aiding-and-abetting elements, including scienter and knowing participation.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Rural/Metro Corp. S'holders Litig., 102 A.3d 205 (Del. Ch. 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Aiders and abettors are jointly and severally liable.

authorities_cited.authority: Ivize of Milwaukee, LLC v. Compex Litig. Support, LLC, 2009 WL 1111179 (Del. Ch. Apr. 27, 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Nominal damages for a breach without proven compensatory harm.

authorities_cited.authority: GB-SP Hldgs., LLC v. Walker, 2024 WL 4799490 (Del. Ch. Nov. 15, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Law of the case bars reviving a claim dismissed with prejudice (applied to Marjo's § 4.11 claim).

authorities_cited.authority: Pers. Touch Hldg. Corp. v. Glaubach, 2019 WL 937180 (Del. Ch. Feb. 25, 2019); Scion Breckenridge Managing Member, LLC v. ASB Allegiance Real Est. Fund, 68 A.3d 665 (Del. 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: American Rule; no fee shifting in a split decision.
Legal rate for pre- and post-judgment interest on fiduciary damages.
Marjo's standing to sue derivatively as a record member.

summary.brief_summary: Post-trial decision by Vice Chancellor Will in consolidated litigation among the co-founders of Accelerant Twister, LLC: Twister and Accelerant Holding, LLC sued Marjo, LLC and John T. Sullivan, who counterclaimed against Twister, Holding, Accelerant Partners and the Founders (Borom, Schuster and Ellman). The Court held that Twister's pretextual for-cause termination of the License Agreement, based on immaterial technical breaches, accelerated the $1 million minimum payment with 18% contractual interest, while Marjo's own breaches warranted only nominal damages. Applying entire fairness under the Second LLC Agreement's capacity-based preservation of Board members' duties, the Court found that the Founders breached their duty of loyalty, aided and abetted by Holding, through the 25% intercompany loan and by diverting Twister's capital raising to Holding, and awarded Marjo direct pro rata damages because Holding owns 83.7% of Twister. The Court upheld the Board-approved unit exchange and the CFG Bank guaranty, dismissed patent-dependent issues under 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a), held the source-code conversion claim preempted, and shifted no fees.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, after trial, (1) Twister validly terminated its License Agreement with Marjo for cause based on technical breaches (no written patent assignment from Sullivan to Marjo; no advance copies of later patent filings), so as to avoid the $1 million minimum payment and § 6.11(d)/(f) consequences; (2) the Founders, as a conflicted majority of Twister's Board, breached their preserved fiduciary duties under § 14.02(c) of the Second LLC Agreement by causing Twister to borrow from Holding at 25% and by diverting Twister's capital-raising opportunities to Holding to escape Marjo's Dilution Protected Units; and (3) what remedy fits where Holding owns 83.7% of Twister.
summary.disposition: judgment in part for each side
summary.holding: Judgment in part for each side. Contract: the License Agreement is valid and enforceable. Marjo committed two immaterial breaches (§ 3.1 assignment representation; § 4.1 advance notice), for which Twister gets $1 in nominal damages, and Twister gets $1 for Marjo's § 11.01(a) breach when Sullivan sent Twister's financial data to prospective litigation funders. The patent filings themselves were not a § 11.01(a) breach because the License Agreement and PLC Contract contemplated them. Because no material breach occurred and the reasons were pretextual, Twister's termination was wrongful and triggered § 6.11(d): Marjo recovers $1,000,000 plus simple 18% interest from January 1, 2023 ($493.15 per day) and post-judgment interest at the contractual rate, plus return of the original PLC prototype, the demonstration unit and the original CAD drawings to the extent in Twister's or Holding's possession, custody or control. An accounting write-off does not show destruction. The PRO2/PRO4 return request and the patent-related portion of Twister and Holding's declaratory claim are dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a). Twister breached § 4.9 through Holding's PaaS business, but Marjo proved only nominal damages ($1). Marjo's § 4.11 claim fails as barred by the with-prejudice dismissal and for lack of proof, and no declaration issues on trade secrets or know-how. Governance: the July 2021 unit exchange was validly approved by a Board majority, but the Revolving Credit Agreement and Intercompany Services Agreement required, and lacked, 90% member approval under § 8.10(i). No standalone Intercompany Services overcharge was proven. Fiduciary: under § 14.02(c), the Founders owed traditional duties when acting as Board members. They failed to prove the 25% Revolving Credit Agreement entirely fair (self-negotiated, undisclosed in advance, rate far above Holding's cost of funds), and they usurped Twister's capital-raising opportunities under all four Broz factors. Because entity-level recovery would flow mostly to Holding and the Founders, Marjo receives direct pro rata damages of $43,142.46 (16.3% of the $264,677.65 overcharge) and $462,000 (Greco's corrected figure), each with pre- and post-judgment interest at the legal rate compounded quarterly. Borom, Schuster, Ellman and Holding are jointly and severally liable, because the Founders' knowledge is imputed to Holding, which aided and abetted the breaches. Holding is barred from collecting any unpaid portion of the overcharge. The CFG Bank guaranty was entirely fair despite the Founders' failure to disclose that CFG first offered the line to Twister, and the CFG usurpation theory fails because Twister could not fund that facility on its own (fn. 456). Twister and Holding's fiduciary claim against Sullivan fails: he acted outside his Board capacity, no additional loss was proven, and dissenting votes are not a breach. Peripheral claims: the conversion claim over the PLC source code is preempted by the Copyright Act, though the fiduciary claim was not preempted (fn. 529). Marjo's Consulting Agreement claim fails because § 2.1 let Twister stop authorizing hourly work and the agreement expired on September 1, 2021. Fees: other than fees previously shifted (April 10, 2026 letter opinion), each side bears its own fees and costs, and unclean hands was declined. The implementing order must state total accrued prejudgment interest, and the parties must confer and submit a form of final order within 30 days.
key_facts_and_concessions: Twister accrued $41,666.67 per month toward the $1 million § 5.2 payment, and the Founders intended to pay it until Sullivan and Marjo's counsel sent a draft complaint on June 23, 2022; the Founders then reversed the accrual, Schuster admitted counsel was hired only afterward to review whether Sullivan "violated" the license, and per instructions received 10/9/2022 legal expenses were applied against the accrual before the October 17, 2022 notice of breach and November 21, 2022 termination.

Sullivan never executed a written assignment of the Provisional Patent Application to Marjo (owned by Sullivan and his spouse), but orally agreed Marjo could license the rights; Borom knew when the License Agreement was signed that Sullivan was the named inventor and applicant and did not ask for a written assignment.

Sullivan sent the September 2020 provisional filings to Twister the day he mailed them, not in advance as § 4.1 required; § 4.1 gave Twister no veto over Marjo's USPTO filings, and Borom forwarded the filings to counsel in December 2020 and raised no concerns for nearly two years.

Schuster signed the 25% Revolving Credit Agreement for both Holding (lender) and Twister (borrower); the Founders approved it over Sullivan's objection, it was never put to the 90% member vote § 8.10(i) requires, and Holding's own cost of funds was 8% (2021 convertible notes) and roughly 10.5% to 12% (CFG line), yielding a $264,677.65 interest spread.

Marjo was the only Twister member asked to forfeit contractual rights (anti-dilution and 90% protective provisions) to join Holding; it declined, and after the July 2021 exchange Holding owned 83.7% of Twister and Marjo 16.3%.

The Founders never attempted a second capital raise in Twister, and there was no credible evidence any investor declined because of Marjo's Dilution Protected Units; Holding raised about $1.7-1.8 million in 2021 notes and $1.2 million in 2022 equity by touting Twister's machines, IP and PaaS model, and its May 2022 PPM even claimed Holding had Dilution Protected Units.
Second LLC Agreement § 14.02(a)-(b) eliminate fiduciary duties for Covered Persons, but § 14.02(c) preserves traditional duties for Board members "while acting in such capacity."

Sullivan and Marjo told the federal court they "do not contend the '627 Patent is infringed" yet sought return of the PRO2 and PRO4 here; Twister and Holding filed a federal non-infringement declaratory action on January 16, 2026 (fn. 290, 294).
summary.practical_takeaway: Where an LLC agreement preserves fiduciary duties for managers acting as board members, founders who restructure through a parent to sidestep a minority member's anti-dilution rights should expect intercompany financing they approve on both sides to be judged under entire fairness against the parent's actual cost of funds, and capital raised on the subsidiary's assets to be treated as a usurped opportunity, with direct pro rata damages to the minority. A licensee that keeps taking a license's benefits cannot later terminate for cause over immaterial breaches it long knew of. Where an "or for any other reason" clause applies, that termination triggers the very acceleration and return obligations it sought to avoid.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial; each proponent bore the burden of proving its claims by a preponderance of the evidence. Entire fairness (burden on the Founders) applied to the Revolving Credit Agreement and the CFG Bank guaranty because the Founders stood on both sides.

entries.name: US INFRA SVCS Buyer, LLC et al v. JDB Capital Partners, LLC et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Plaintiffs' request for a pretrial hearing to impose adverse inferences: denied. The Rule 37(e)(2) state-of-mind assessment is typically made after hearing the evidence at trial and could not be made on the paper record.
Implicit premise that prejudice and remedy can be fixed pretrial: rejected. The complete trial record will let the Court evaluate any resulting prejudice and tailor a proportionate remedy.

Need for pre-merits evidentiary rulings: rejected. In a bench trial the Court need not issue preliminary evidentiary instructions to itself and can decide any adverse inference or burden shift while deciding the merits.

authorities_cited.proposition: An adverse inference requires a finding that the party acted recklessly or with intent to deprive another party of the information's use in the litigation.

authorities_cited.authority: Beard Rsch., Inc. v. Kates, 981 A.2d 1175 (Del. Ch. 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Negligent destruction does not warrant an adverse inference. Spoliation remedies must be tailored to culpability and prejudice, and consideration of additional adverse inferences may be deferred to post-trial briefing and argument.

authorities_cited.authority: Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. Midcap, 893 A.2d 542 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted through Beard: an adverse inference requires a preliminary finding of intentional or reckless destruction of evidence.

authorities_cited.authority: Fortis Advisors, LLC v. Johnson & Johnson, C.A. No. 2020-0881-LWW (Del. Ch. June 5, 2023) (TRANSCRIPT)
authorities_cited.proposition: The court could not make credibility determinations or assess an alleged spoliator's state of mind pretrial.

authorities_cited.authority: Goldstein v. Denner, 310 A.3d 548 (Del. Ch. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: If a motion turns on evidentiary issues the court will evaluate at trial, it makes sense to defer the motion until trial.

authorities_cited.authority: Gener8, LLC v. Castanon, 2023 WL 6381635 (Del. Ch. Sept. 29, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Rule 37(e) motion was resolved in a post-trial opinion, with tailored adverse inferences drawn after live evaluation of witness credibility.

summary.brief_summary: Six weeks before trial, Plaintiffs (US INFRA SVCS Buyer, LLC et al.) moved for Rule 37(e)(2) adverse inferences against Defendants (JDB Capital Partners, LLC et al.). They alleged that a defendant's trustee failed to disable auto-delete, failed to preserve phone data during upgrades, and deleted texts, and they asked for a pretrial hearing. Vice Chancellor Will denied the hearing request and deferred the Motion to the post-trial decision. The Court observed a growing influx of pre-merits spoliation motions and reasoned that the required recklessness-or-intent finding and the assessment of prejudice and remedy depend on credibility and the full trial record. It added that a bench-trial court need not instruct itself in advance.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether the Court should convene a pretrial hearing to impose Ct. Ch. R. 37(e)(2) adverse inferences for alleged spoliation in a bench-tried case, or defer the spoliation motion to the post-trial decision, where the predicate state-of-mind finding (recklessness or intent to deprive) cannot be made on the paper record.

flags.assertion: The case will be tried to the bench, so no preliminary evidentiary instruction is needed.
flags.evidence: In a bench trial, the court need not issue preliminary evidentiary instructions to itself.
flags.opinion_says: The letter says bench-trial courts need not issue preliminary instructions to themselves, but does not say the case will be tried to the bench or that no instruction is needed here.
flags.problem: The opinion states a general principle about bench trials but never says this case is a bench trial.

summary.holding: The Court denied Plaintiffs' request for a pretrial hearing to impose adverse inferences and deferred the Motion to the post-trial decision. Whether the trustee's conduct was negligent, reckless or intentional cannot be determined on the paper record. The full trial record will allow the Court to assess prejudice and tailor a proportionate remedy. In a bench trial, the Court can decide any adverse inference or burden shift together with the merits. The parties may complete their stipulated pretrial briefing, but they should present evidence on the alleged spoliation at trial and address the requested relief in post-trial briefing.
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiffs moved on October 16, 2026 for adverse inferences due to spoliation (Dkt. 351), with trial six weeks away, and asked the Court to convene a pretrial hearing to impose them.
Plaintiffs assert that a defendant's trustee failed to disable cell phone auto-delete settings, failed to preserve data during phone upgrades, and deleted text messages.
The Court found it could not resolve on the existing paper record whether that conduct reflects negligence, recklessness or intentional spoliation.
The case will be tried to the bench, so no preliminary evidentiary instruction is needed.
The parties have stipulated pretrial briefing on the Motion.
summary.practical_takeaway: In Chancery bench trials, expect Rule 37(e)(2) adverse-inference motions that turn on the alleged spoliator's state of mind to be deferred to the post-trial decision. Develop the spoliation evidence, especially live testimony on intent or recklessness and on prejudice, for presentation at trial, and brief the requested remedy post-trial rather than relying on a pretrial ruling.
summary.standard_of_review: Not stated as a standard of review. The Court noted that Ct. Ch. R. 37(e)(2) requires a finding that the party acted "recklessly or with the intent to deprive another party of the information's use in the litigation" before an adverse inference may be drawn.
